title: College Prep English 1 & 2 (12th Grade)
description: College prep English - literature, composition, rhetoric

questions.question: Identify the author of 'The Great Gatsby.'
questions.explanation: F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby in 1925, the defining novel of the Jazz Age.
questions.memoryHook: Gatsby raises a green-light toast, and Fitzgerald picks up the tab!

questions.question: In APA style, which is the correct parenthetical in-text citation for a direct quotation from page 45 of a 2020 book by Dana Ruiz?
questions.explanation: An APA parenthetical citation gives the author's last name only, the year, and - for a direct quotation - the page shown as p. 45, with the parts separated by commas.
questions.memoryHook: APA stacks it neat - last name, year, page, like a tiny bookshelf!

questions.question: Which novel features the character Atticus Finch?
questions.explanation: Atticus Finch is the principled lawyer father in Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird (1960).
questions.memoryHook: Atticus stands tall in the courtroom - mockingbirds sing for the innocent!

questions.question: Identify the author of the poem 'The Raven.'
questions.explanation: Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Raven' in 1845, famous for its refrain 'Nevermore.'
questions.memoryHook: Nevermore! Poe's raven croaks the author's name all night!

questions.question: Before drafting, a writer lists her main points in order and groups her supporting details under each one. Which prewriting strategy is she using?
questions.explanation: An outline arranges main points and their supporting details in order before drafting begins. Freewriting is unstructured timed writing with no organization, while proofreading and peer review happen only after a draft exists.
questions.memoryHook: An outline is the treasure map you draw before the dig!

questions.question: Identify the author of 'Their Eyes Were Watching God.'
questions.explanation: Zora Neale Hurston, a key Harlem Renaissance figure, published Their Eyes Were Watching God in 1937.
questions.memoryHook: Hurston's eyes watch from Eatonville - Zora saw it all!

questions.question: In an APA reference list, which entry correctly formats a print book by Miguel Santos, published in 2019 by Harbor Press, titled The Working River?
questions.correctAnswer: Santos, M. (2019). The working river. Harbor Press.
distractors: Santos, Miguel. (2019). The Working River. Harbor Press.
Santos, M. (2019). The Working River. Harbor Press.
Santos, M. 2019. The working river. Harbor Press.
questions.explanation: An APA book reference lists the author's last name and initials, the year in parentheses, the book title in sentence case (only the first word and proper nouns capitalized), and then the publisher.
questions.memoryHook: In APA, book titles whisper - sentence case, only the first word stands tall!

questions.question: Which author is most closely associated with Transcendentalism?
questions.explanation: Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 'Self-Reliance' is a cornerstone of Transcendentalist thought.
questions.memoryHook: Emerson transcends - self-reliance lifts you above the crowd!

questions.question: A student rewrites her science report for the school newspaper instead of her chemistry teacher. In the rhetorical situation, what has mainly changed?
questions.explanation: The readers changed - from an expert teacher to general student readers - so the language, examples, and explanations must change with them. The topic (her science results) and the purpose (reporting findings) stay the same.
questions.memoryHook: Same report, new readers - know who is listening before you roar!

questions.question: Identify the author of 'Beloved.'
questions.explanation: Toni Morrison won the Pulitzer Prize for Beloved (1987); she later won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
questions.memoryHook: Morrison's Beloved haunts - Toni tells the story that won't stay buried!

questions.question: Identify the author of 'Pride and Prejudice.'
questions.explanation: Jane Austen published Pride and Prejudice in 1813, featuring Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy.
questions.memoryHook: Austen minds the manners - pride meets prejudice at the ball!

questions.question: Identify the author of '1984.'
questions.explanation: George Orwell published the dystopian novel 1984 in 1949, introducing Big Brother and Newspeak.
questions.memoryHook: Big Brother is watching - Orwell's 1984 never blinks!

questions.question: A city council member writes a letter urging residents to support a new library tax. What is the writer's main purpose in this rhetorical situation?
questions.correctAnswer: To persuade residents to support the tax
distractors: To entertain residents with a story
To record the council's meeting minutes
To explain how property taxes are calculated
questions.explanation: Purpose is what a writer wants the audience to think or do. Urging residents to support a tax asks them to take a position and act, which is persuasion, not merely informing or recording.
questions.memoryHook: When a writer wants you to DO something, the purpose is persuasion!

questions.question: Choose the sentence with the correct apostrophe use.
questions.correctAnswer: My sister's car needs new brakes.
distractors: My sisters car needs new brakes.
My sister's car needs new brake's.
My sisters' car need's new brakes.
questions.explanation: A singular possessive takes an apostrophe plus s: one sister owns the car, so it is sister's car. Plain plurals such as brakes never take an apostrophe.
questions.memoryHook: One sister, one apostrophe before the s - sister's car, easy claw-scratch!

questions.question: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
questions.correctAnswer: The rain stopped, and the game resumed.
distractors: The rain stopped and, the game resumed.
The rain stopped, the game resumed.
The rain stopped; and the game resumed.
questions.explanation: When the conjunction 'and' joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction. A comma by itself creates a comma splice, and a semicolon is not paired with 'and'.
questions.memoryHook: Comma first, then 'and' - the FANBOYS bridge needs its comma plank!

questions.question: Identify the author of 'Lord of the Flies.'
questions.explanation: William Golding published Lord of the Flies in 1954, about schoolboys stranded on an island.
questions.memoryHook: The flies buzz on the island - Golding rules the stranded boys!

questions.question: Read the passage from Jane Austen's 'Pride and Prejudice' (1813): "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters." Which statement best captures the main idea of the passage?
questions.correctAnswer: Neighbors assume that any wealthy single man who arrives is a future husband for a local daughter
distractors: Wealthy men actively search for wives when they move to a new neighborhood
The narrator proves that all rich men want to get married
Families in the neighborhood resent wealthy newcomers
questions.explanation: Austen says the belief is fixed in the minds of the surrounding families even though the man's own feelings are little known. The passage is about the neighbors' assumption - delivered with irony - not about what wealthy men actually want.
questions.memoryHook: Austen's neighbors had the wedding planned before the gentleman unpacked!

questions.question: Determine the historical event that 'Animal Farm' allegorizes.
questions.explanation: Orwell's Animal Farm (1945) satirizes the Russian Revolution, with the pigs as Bolshevik leaders.
questions.memoryHook: The pigs take the farm - Orwell's animals replay the Revolution!

questions.question: Read the passage: "When the city's first public library opened in 1911, it stayed open only four hours a day, and children were not allowed inside at all. Librarian Ada Brooks changed that. She set aside a corner with low shelves, persuaded the board to add evening hours, and started a Saturday reading club. Within five years, the library's youngest members outnumbered its adult ones." What is the main idea of the passage?
questions.correctAnswer: One librarian's changes turned a restricted library into a place where children became the majority of members
distractors: Public libraries in 1911 were usually managed by women
The library board opposed every change Ada Brooks proposed
Children in 1911 preferred reading clubs to going to school
questions.explanation: Every detail supports one arc: the library began restricted, Brooks changed its rules and spaces, and children then outnumbered adults. The board detail is wrong as stated - she persuaded the board, so it did not oppose every change.
questions.memoryHook: The main idea is the whole story in one bite - Ada opened the library doors to kids!

questions.question: Which task belongs to revision rather than editing?
questions.correctAnswer: Reorganizing paragraphs so the argument builds in a clearer order
distractors: Fixing a misspelled word in the introduction
Adding a missing comma before a quotation
Correcting the capitalization of a proper noun
questions.explanation: Revision works on ideas, organization, and development - it is the re-seeing stage of writing. Spelling, commas, and capitalization are editing and proofreading concerns, handled after the larger issues are settled.
questions.memoryHook: Revise the big bones first - commas can wait their turn!

questions.question: Which term best describes a recurring object that represents an abstract idea?
questions.explanation: A symbol is a concrete object standing for an abstract idea, like a dove for peace.
questions.memoryHook: A dove means peace - symbols wear costumes as ideas!

questions.question: Identify the term for the main character who drives the plot.
questions.explanation: The protagonist is the central character whose goals drive the story forward.
questions.memoryHook: The protagonist leads the parade - follow the main figure!

questions.question: Which term best describes a character who contrasts with another to highlight traits?
questions.explanation: A foil's contrasting qualities throw the main character's traits into sharper relief.
questions.memoryHook: A foil is the shiny opposite - contrast makes characters pop!

questions.question: Identify the term for the turning point of a story's plot.
questions.explanation: The climax is the moment of highest tension where the central conflict turns.
questions.memoryHook: The climax is the mountain top - the plot can't climb higher!

questions.question: Which term best describes a story's time and place?
questions.explanation: Setting is the when and where of a narrative; mood is the feeling it creates.
questions.memoryHook: Setting sets the stage - time and place paint the backdrop!

questions.question: Determine the term for the central message or insight of a work.
questions.explanation: Theme is the underlying message about life or human nature, distinct from plot events.
questions.memoryHook: The theme is the treasure - dig under the plot to find it!

questions.question: Identify which pronouns a first-person singular narrator uses.
questions.explanation: First-person singular narration uses I/me/my (the first-person plural forms are we/us/our); second person uses you; third person uses he/she/they.
questions.memoryHook: I tell my own tale - first person keeps it personal!

questions.question: Which term best describes a comparison using 'like' or 'as'?
questions.explanation: A simile compares two things with like or as; a metaphor states the comparison directly.
questions.memoryHook: Like, as - similes compare with training wheels!

questions.question: Identify the term for giving human qualities to nonhuman things.
questions.explanation: Personification attributes human traits to objects or ideas, like 'the wind whispered.'
questions.memoryHook: The wind whispers - personification gives things a voice!

questions.question: Which term best describes extreme exaggeration used for effect?
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate overstatement, as in 'I've told you a million times.'
questions.memoryHook: A million times over - hyperbole never does anything small!

questions.question: In rhetoric, determine what ethos appeals to in an audience.
questions.explanation: Ethos builds trust through the speaker's character, expertise, and credibility.
questions.memoryHook: Trust the badge - ethos flashes credentials!

questions.question: In rhetoric, determine what pathos appeals to in an audience.
questions.explanation: Pathos persuades by stirring feelings such as sympathy, anger, or hope.
questions.memoryHook: Pathos pulls heartstrings - feel the argument!

questions.question: In rhetoric, determine what logos appeals to in an audience.
questions.explanation: Logos relies on evidence, facts, and logical reasoning to persuade.
questions.memoryHook: Logos loves logic - numbers and reasons rule!

questions.question: Identify the rhetorical device in which a speaker says the opposite of what they mean for effect.
questions.explanation: Verbal irony is a statement whose intended meaning is the opposite of its literal words.
questions.memoryHook: Say the opposite with a wink - verbal irony talks backwards!

questions.question: Which term best describes dramatic irony, when the audience knows something a character does not?
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony creates tension because viewers know more than the characters on stage.
questions.memoryHook: You know, they don't - dramatic irony keeps secrets from the stage!

questions.question: Identify the rhetorical device of repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses.
questions.explanation: Anaphora repeats openings, as in 'I have a dream... I have a dream' from Dr. King.
questions.memoryHook: I have a dream, I have a dream - anaphora repeats the drumbeat!

questions.question: Which term best describes a question asked for effect rather than an answer?
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question makes a point; the speaker does not expect a reply.
questions.memoryHook: Who needs an answer? Rhetorical questions ask for effect!

questions.question: Identify the logical fallacy of misrepresenting an opponent's argument to attack the weaker version.
questions.explanation: A straw man distorts the other side's position into an easier target to knock down.
questions.memoryHook: Don't fight a straw man - attack the real argument!

questions.question: Identify the logical fallacy of attacking the person instead of their argument.
questions.explanation: Ad hominem means 'to the person' - it dodges the argument by insulting the arguer.
questions.memoryHook: Argue the point, not the person - ad hominem misses the target!

questions.question: Determine the rhetorical device used in 'I came, I saw, I conquered.'
questions.explanation: Parallelism repeats the same grammatical structure across clauses for rhythm and force.
questions.memoryHook: March in step - parallel structure keeps clauses in formation!

questions.question: Determine where a thesis statement usually appears in an essay.
questions.correctAnswer: at the end of the introduction
distractors: at the start of the introduction
in the middle of the body
questions.explanation: Placing the thesis at the end of the introduction lets context build before the main claim lands.
questions.memoryHook: The thesis lands the intro - last line, main claim!

questions.question: Which best describes a counterargument in an essay?
questions.correctAnswer: an opposing view the writer addresses
questions.explanation: Acknowledging a counterargument shows fairness and lets the writer answer objections.
questions.memoryHook: Hear the other side - counterarguments steel-man the opposition!

questions.question: Determine the function of a rebuttal in an essay.
questions.correctAnswer: responds to and refutes a counterargument
questions.explanation: After raising a counterargument, the rebuttal explains why it fails or is outweighed.
questions.memoryHook: Rebuttal roars back - answer the objection and move on!

questions.question: Which is the strongest thesis statement?
questions.correctAnswer: School uniforms limit student self-expression and should be optional.
questions.explanation: A strong thesis is specific and arguable; the others are vague, announcing, or factual.
questions.memoryHook: A thesis takes a stand - arguable and specific wins!

questions.question: Determine the function of topic sentences in body paragraphs.
questions.correctAnswer: introduce the main idea of a paragraph
questions.explanation: Each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence that connects its point to the thesis.
questions.memoryHook: Every paragraph needs a captain - the topic sentence leads!

questions.question: Determine the primary function of transitions between paragraphs.
distractors: repeat the thesis word for word
questions.explanation: Transitions signal how ideas connect - contrast, cause, sequence, or addition.
questions.memoryHook: Transitions are bridges - ideas cross without falling!

questions.question: Identify what a writer should NOT do in a conclusion.
questions.explanation: New evidence belongs in the body; the conclusion synthesizes what was already argued.
questions.memoryHook: The conclusion wraps the gift - no new surprises inside!

questions.question: Determine how a writer mainly builds ethos in an essay.
questions.explanation: Credible sources show the writer is informed and trustworthy, strengthening ethos.
questions.memoryHook: Cite the experts - borrowed credibility boosts your ethos!

questions.question: Choose the strongest primary evidence for a literary analysis essay.
questions.explanation: Direct textual evidence grounds claims about literature better than outside commentary.
questions.memoryHook: Let the text testify - quotes are your star witnesses!

questions.question: Determine the defining feature of a synthesis essay.
questions.correctAnswer: combines multiple sources into a new argument
questions.explanation: Synthesis weaves sources together so their combination produces an original claim.
questions.memoryHook: Synthesis stirs the pot - blend sources into something new!

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'If I ___ taller, I would play basketball.'
questions.explanation: The subjunctive mood uses 'were' for wishes and hypotheticals, even with singular subjects.
questions.memoryHook: Wish upon were - the subjunctive dreams in were!

questions.question: Choose the parallel option: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and ___.'
questions.explanation: Parallel structure keeps all items in the same form - three gerunds here.
questions.memoryHook: Hiking, swimming, reading - keep the -ing parade uniform!

questions.question: Identify the error in 'Running quickly, the finish line approached.'
questions.correctAnswer: The modifier dangles - the finish line was not running.
questions.explanation: The participial phrase must modify the subject, but the subject here cannot run.
questions.memoryHook: Who is running? Modifiers must cling to the right noun!

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the teacher nor the students ___ ready.'
questions.explanation: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject - the plural 'students.'
questions.memoryHook: The verb hugs the nearer subject - students were ready!

questions.question: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Between you and ___, this test is hard.'
questions.explanation: Prepositions take object pronouns - 'between you and me' is correct.
questions.memoryHook: Prepositions love objects - between you and me!

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The storm ended; ___, the streets were flooded.'
questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb like 'however' follows a semicolon to join two independent clauses.
questions.memoryHook: Semicolon plus however - a fancy pause with manners!

questions.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The committee ___ reached its decision.'
questions.explanation: A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb.
questions.memoryHook: The committee acts as one - singular group, singular verb!

questions.question: Which sentence best demonstrates the subjunctive mood?
questions.correctAnswer: I suggest that he study harder.
questions.explanation: Verbs like suggest, demand, and insist trigger the subjunctive - base form 'study,' not 'studies.'
questions.memoryHook: Suggest, demand, insist - then drop the s!

questions.question: Identify the error in 'She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.'
questions.correctAnswer: The modifier is misplaced - the plates could describe the children.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'on paper plates' sits next to 'children,' creating unintended humor.
questions.memoryHook: Park the modifier next to its noun - no wandering phrases!

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The new policy will ___ test scores.'
questions.explanation: 'Affect' is usually the verb meaning to influence; 'effect' is usually the noun meaning result.
questions.memoryHook: Affect is the action - A for action, E for the noun effect!

questions.question: Which definition best matches 'cogent' in the sentence: 'The author's argument was cogent.'
questions.explanation: A cogent argument is clear, logical, and persuasive.
questions.memoryHook: Cogent is convincing - a cogent case clicks shut!

questions.question: In APA style, which sentence uses the correct narrative in-text citation for a source by Lopez and Chen published in 2021?
questions.correctAnswer: Lopez and Chen (2021) found that sleep predicted recall.
distractors: Lopez & Chen (2021) found that sleep predicted recall.
Lopez et al. (2021) found that sleep predicted recall.
Lopez and Chen, 2021, found that sleep predicted recall.
questions.explanation: In a narrative citation, APA spells out the word 'and' and names both authors when a source has exactly two. The ampersand (&) belongs only inside parentheses, and 'et al.' is reserved for sources with three or more authors.
questions.memoryHook: Two authors, both names - 'and' in the sentence, '&' only in parentheses!

questions.question: Which definition best matches 'pragmatic' in the sentence: 'They chose a pragmatic solution.'
questions.explanation: Pragmatic means guided by practical results rather than theory.
questions.memoryHook: Pragmatic is practical - fix the fence, skip the philosophy!

questions.question: Which entry is the correct APA reference-list format for a journal article by Priya Nair and Tom Ellis, published in 2022 in the Journal of School Research, volume 14, issue 2, pages 120-131?
questions.correctAnswer: Nair, P., & Ellis, T. (2022). Sleep and memory in teens. Journal of School Research, 14(2), 120-131.
distractors: Nair, Priya, & Ellis, Tom. (2022). Sleep and memory in teens. Journal of School Research, 14(2), 120-131.
Nair, P., & Ellis, T. (2022). Sleep And Memory In Teens. Journal of School Research, 14(2), 120-131.
Nair, P., & Ellis, T. (2022). Sleep and memory in teens. Journal of School Research, 14, pp. 120-131.
questions.explanation: An APA journal reference uses authors' last names and initials, the article title in sentence case, the journal title in title case, the volume followed by the issue in parentheses, and the page range with no 'pp.' in the reference list.
questions.memoryHook: Initials, sentence-case title, volume(issue), pages - the APA journal recipe!

questions.question: Which definition best matches 'magnanimous' in the sentence: 'The magnanimous winner praised her opponent.'
questions.explanation: Magnanimous means noble and generous, especially toward a rival.
questions.memoryHook: Magnanimous is mega-generous - big heart, big winner!

questions.question: After three students are injured at the crosswalk outside school, a student writes an editorial demanding a traffic light at the intersection. In rhetorical terms, the injuries are best described as the editorial's:
questions.correctAnswer: Exigence - the problem that prompts the writing
distractors: Audience - the people the writer hopes to reach
Constraint - a limit on what the writer can say or do
Genre - the category the text belongs to
questions.explanation: Exigence is the urgent problem or occasion that calls a text into being; here, the injuries created the need for the editorial. The audience would be the readers and decision-makers, constraints are limits on the writer, and the genre is 'editorial'.
questions.memoryHook: Exigence is the spark - the problem that makes the writer pick up the pen!

questions.question: Which definition best matches 'tenuous' in the sentence: 'The link between the events was tenuous.'
questions.explanation: Tenuous describes something flimsy with little substance.
questions.memoryHook: Tenuous is thin - a spider thread of a link!

questions.question: A graduation speech written in 2020 praises a class that 'learned to learn from kitchen tables and laptop screens.' A reader in 2070 might misunderstand the speech without knowing its:
questions.correctAnswer: Context - the circumstances and events surrounding its creation
distractors: Purpose - what the speaker wanted the audience to feel
Audience - the people the speech was written for
Figurative language - the images and comparisons it uses
questions.explanation: Context is the situation around a text. The phrase only makes sense against the events of 2020, when schools closed and students learned from home; a future reader who lacks that background knowledge can misread the reference even with the words in front of them.
questions.memoryHook: Context is the world around the words - kitchen-table school only makes sense in 2020!

questions.question: Choose the sentence that uses a semicolon correctly.
questions.correctAnswer: The museum was crowded; even so, we stayed until closing.
distractors: The museum was crowded; and we stayed until closing.
The museum was; crowded even so we stayed.
The museum was crowded, even so; we stayed until closing.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. A transitional phrase such as 'even so' can follow the semicolon and is set off with a comma; a semicolon cannot split a subject from its verb or pair with 'and'.
questions.memoryHook: A semicolon is a full stop with a wink - two whole sentences, closely linked!

questions.question: Which revision correctly fixes the comma splice in this sentence? 'The experiment failed, the team changed its approach.'
questions.correctAnswer: The experiment failed, so the team changed its approach.
distractors: The experiment failed the team changed its approach.
The experiment failed; the team changed, its approach.
The experiment failed, the team changed, its approach.
questions.explanation: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. Adding a coordinating conjunction such as 'so' after the comma fixes it (a semicolon or a period also works); removing the comma creates a fused sentence instead.
questions.memoryHook: Two sentences stuck on one little comma? Add a 'so' bridge or split them up!

questions.question: A student paraphrases an idea from a 2018 source by Ortiz entirely in her own words, without quoting it. In APA style, what must she still do?
questions.correctAnswer: Cite Ortiz (2018) in the text, because paraphrased ideas still require credit
distractors: Nothing - citations are only required for direct quotations
List the source in the reference list but never mention it in the text
Put the paraphrase in quotation marks and add a page number
questions.explanation: APA requires an in-text citation for paraphrases as well as for direct quotations, because the idea still belongs to the source. A page number is encouraged for a paraphrase but not required, and quotation marks are used only for exact wording.
questions.memoryHook: Your words, their idea - APA still wants the credit tag!

questions.question: Determine the rhyme scheme of a Shakespearean sonnet.
questions.explanation: The English sonnet uses three quatrains and a closing couplet: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.
questions.memoryHook: Three quatrains plus a couplet - Shakespeare's recipe!

questions.question: A charity drafts a fundraising email in January but sends it the week after a hurricane strikes the region it serves, and donations triple. Which rhetorical concept best explains why the timing mattered?
questions.correctAnswer: Kairos - the timeliness and opportune moment for a message
distractors: Ethos - the credibility of the sender
Logos - the logic of the argument
Pathos - the emotional content of the appeal
questions.explanation: Kairos is the opportune moment for a message. The email's words did not change; sending them when the audience was focused on the disaster made the same appeal far more effective. Pathos names the emotional content itself, not the timing of its delivery.
questions.memoryHook: Kairos means striking while the moment is hot - timing is a rhetorical tool!

questions.question: Identify the metrical foot of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.
questions.explanation: The iamb (da-DUM) is the most common foot in English verse.
questions.memoryHook: Da-DUM, da-DUM - the iamb hops like a heartbeat!

questions.question: Which term best describes a poem mourning the dead?
questions.explanation: An elegy is a formal lament for someone who has died.
questions.memoryHook: An elegy weeps in verse - mourning set to meter!

questions.question: Determine the meaning of enjambment in poetry.
questions.correctAnswer: a sentence running past a line break without punctuation
distractors: a rhyme at the ends of lines
a pause in the middle of a line
questions.explanation: Enjambment carries the sense over the line ending, pulling the reader forward.
questions.memoryHook: Enjambment jumps the line - the sentence leaps the break!

questions.question: In Carl Sandburg's 'Fog,' determine the figurative device in the line 'comes on little cat feet.'
questions.explanation: The fog is directly compared to a cat without like or as, making it a metaphor.
questions.memoryHook: Fog on cat feet - Sandburg's metaphor pads in silently!

questions.question: In Frost's 'The Road Not Taken,' determine what the two roads most likely symbolize.
questions.explanation: The forked roads are a classic symbol for decisions that shape a life.
questions.memoryHook: Two roads diverged - Frost's fork is life's choices!

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated so that it means the writer has more than one brother?
questions.correctAnswer: My brother Daniel lives in Ohio.
distractors: My brother, Daniel, lives in Ohio.
My brother Daniel, lives in Ohio.
My, brother Daniel, lives in Ohio.
questions.explanation: Without commas, the name restricts which brother is meant, implying there are several brothers and one must be identified. Commas around 'Daniel' would make the name nonessential extra information, which implies he is the writer's only brother.
questions.memoryHook: No commas means 'the Daniel one of my brothers' - commas would make him an only child!

questions.question: Which statement best describes the defining feature of free verse?
questions.explanation: Free verse abandons fixed patterns, using natural speech rhythms instead.
questions.memoryHook: Free verse runs wild - no rhyme, no meter, no cage!

questions.question: Read the passage from Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address (1863): "Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. Now we are engaged in a great civil war, testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure." What is Lincoln's main purpose in this excerpt?
questions.correctAnswer: To frame the Civil War as a test of whether a nation founded on equality can survive
distractors: To announce a new law freeing enslaved people
To describe the fighting that took place at Gettysburg
To criticize the founders for building the nation on a weak idea
questions.explanation: Lincoln defines the nation by its founding proposition - equality - and calls the war a test of whether such a nation can long endure. The excerpt announces no law, describes no battle, and honors rather than criticizes the founding idea.
questions.memoryHook: Lincoln zooms out - the war is a test of the nation's founding promise!

questions.question: Identify the play containing the line 'To be, or not to be.'
questions.explanation: Hamlet speaks the famous soliloquy in Act 3 while contemplating life and death.
questions.memoryHook: To be or not to be - Hamlet ponders on the ramparts!

questions.question: In 'Romeo and Juliet,' determine which house Romeo belongs to.
questions.explanation: Romeo is a Montague; Juliet is a Capulet - the feuding houses of Verona.
questions.memoryHook: Montague meets Capulet - feuding families, fatal love!

questions.question: Read the passage from Frederick Douglass's 'Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass' (1845): "I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland. I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it." What can the reader infer from Douglass's statement that he has no accurate knowledge of his age?
questions.correctAnswer: Slaveholders deliberately kept enslaved people ignorant of basic facts about themselves
distractors: Douglass simply forgot his birth date as he grew older
No birth records existed anywhere in Maryland at the time
Douglass chose not to ask anyone when he was born
questions.explanation: Douglass's missing birth date was not forgetfulness or personal choice: slaveholders withheld such records on purpose, because keeping enslaved people ignorant of their own identities was one way the system maintained control over them.
questions.memoryHook: Not knowing your own birthday was no accident - it was part of the chains.

questions.question: In 'Macbeth,' determine what Lady Macbeth's 'Out, damned spot!' refers to.
questions.explanation: Sleepwalking Lady Macbeth tries to wash invisible blood - guilt made visible.
questions.memoryHook: Out, damned spot - Lady Macbeth scrubs the guilt!

questions.question: Read the passage: "Urban trees do more than decorate sidewalks. A mature street tree can intercept hundreds of gallons of stormwater a year, slowing runoff into storm drains. Its shade can lower the temperature of nearby pavement by several degrees on summer afternoons. Some species, however, drop fruit that litters walkways, and roots can crack pavement if the planting pit is too small." A writer claims: 'Street trees help cities manage stormwater.' Which sentence from the passage best supports the claim?
questions.correctAnswer: A mature street tree can intercept hundreds of gallons of stormwater a year, slowing runoff into storm drains.
distractors: Its shade can lower the temperature of nearby pavement by several degrees on summer afternoons.
Some species, however, drop fruit that litters walkways, and roots can crack pavement if the planting pit is too small.
Urban trees do more than decorate sidewalks.
questions.explanation: Evidence must match the claim's specific point. Only the stormwater sentence addresses stormwater directly; the shade sentence supports a different benefit, and the last sentence states a drawback rather than support.
questions.memoryHook: Match the evidence to the exact claim - stormwater claim, stormwater proof!

questions.question: A student's draft thesis reads: 'Social media is bad for teenagers in many ways.' Which revision makes the strongest thesis statement?
questions.correctAnswer: Because social media platforms are designed to reward constant checking, they fragment teenagers' attention and undermine the sustained focus that schoolwork requires.
distractors: Social media is very bad for teenagers and should be banned everywhere immediately.
This essay will discuss some positive and negative effects of social media on teenagers.
Teenagers use social media a lot, and it affects them in different ways.
questions.explanation: A strong thesis makes a specific, arguable claim and signals the reasoning behind it. The key names a mechanism (design that rewards checking) and its consequence (fragmented attention); the others stay vague, merely announce the essay, or state a fact without taking a position.
questions.memoryHook: A strong thesis takes a side AND shows its 'because'!

questions.question: Identify the villain who drives the plot of 'Othello.'
questions.explanation: Iago's scheming destroys Othello through jealousy and manipulation.
questions.memoryHook: Iago whispers poison - Othello's villain smiles while he schemes!

questions.question: Determine how a Shakespearean tragedy typically ends.
questions.explanation: Tragedy follows the hero's fatal flaw to a catastrophic, usually fatal, close.
questions.memoryHook: Tragedies fall hard - the hero falls with the curtain!

questions.question: Read the paragraph: "(1) Remote work has changed how companies think about office space. (2) Many firms now rent smaller offices because employees come in only two or three days a week. (3) This shift has cut spending on rent and utilities. (4) My cousin grows tomatoes on her apartment balcony every summer. (5) As a result, downtown landlords are redesigning buildings to attract flexible tenants." Which sentence breaks the paragraph's unity and should be removed during revision?
questions.explanation: Every sentence in a unified paragraph develops one controlling idea - here, remote work reshaping office space. Sentence 4 introduces an unrelated topic (balcony tomatoes), so revision removes it; the other sentences all support or conclude the main point.
questions.memoryHook: One paragraph, one party - the tomato sentence wandered in from another garden!

questions.question: In MLA style, determine the correct format of an in-text citation for a book by one author.
questions.explanation: MLA uses author last name and page number with no comma: (Smith 42).
questions.memoryHook: Name and page in parentheses - MLA keeps it lean: (Smith 42)!

questions.question: Determine what an MLA Works Cited page lists.
questions.correctAnswer: every source cited in the paper
questions.explanation: Works Cited includes exactly the sources referenced in-text - no more, no fewer.
questions.memoryHook: Cited means listed - if it's in the paper, it's on the page!

questions.question: Which of the following best describes plagiarism?
questions.explanation: Ideas need attribution even when restated; citations and common knowledge are safe.
questions.memoryHook: Credit every borrow - uncredited ideas are stolen snacks!

questions.question: Choose the best example of a primary source for a history research paper.
questions.correctAnswer: A diary written during the time period
questions.explanation: Primary sources are firsthand accounts from the era; the others interpret them.
questions.memoryHook: Primary means firsthand - a diary from the day beats a textbook!

questions.question: Choose the best thesis for a research paper.
questions.explanation: A research thesis makes a debatable claim narrow enough to prove with evidence.
questions.memoryHook: A thesis with teeth - specific, arguable, ready to defend!

questions.question: In MLA Works Cited, determine what a 'hanging indent' means.
questions.correctAnswer: first line flush left, remaining lines indented
questions.explanation: The hanging indent makes authors' names easy to scan down the left margin.
questions.memoryHook: First line out, rest in - the hanging indent dangles!

questions.question: Determine what you must do when you paraphrase a source.
distractors: do nothing - they are your words now
questions.explanation: Paraphrases restate ideas, but the ideas still belong to the source - cite them.
questions.memoryHook: New words, same debt - paraphrases need citations too!

questions.question: Choose the source most likely credible for academic research.
questions.explanation: Peer review means experts vetted the work before publication.
questions.memoryHook: Peers check the work - journals earn the trust badge!

questions.question: Determine the purpose of an annotated bibliography.
questions.explanation: Each annotation briefly describes the source and judges its usefulness.
questions.memoryHook: Annotate means assess - summarize and judge each source!

questions.question: Determine what synthesis means in research writing.
questions.correctAnswer: combining sources to form a new insight
questions.explanation: Synthesis goes beyond summary - sources interact to support an original claim.
questions.memoryHook: Synthesis is alchemy - blend sources into gold!
